title: Once Upon a Quick Stop
tagline: Keep the shopping. Summon the trouble.
premise: The Host gives you a boring weekday errand and a fairy tale opening. Turn the errand into the first paragraph of a story, while keeping the errand's two ordinary things real. Make it magical, rude, romantic or gloriously doomed, but do not lose the shopping.

seed_pool.opening_token: Once, on a very ordinary Tuesday...

opening: Once, on a very ordinary Tuesday...
Long ago, on the high street...
At the edge of the enchanted town...
Before the clock struck half past nine...
In a land ruled by one tired queen...
On the morning the pigeons spoke...

tests: One short line or sentence, under the word limit. A stranger sees the tale begin at once.
It names exactly two ordinary errand objects or items, each with a clear job in the errand.
It uses the opening cue or its unmistakable words, so the line feels like a fairy tale opening rather than a shop update.
The errand is harmless and checkable. No real brands, public figures, graphic harm or impossible shopping list.
There is room for enchantment, danger, romance or nonsense, but the two small errands remain visible inside the spell.

move_constraints.example: In the kingdom, Ella returned a library book and bought toothpaste from a dragon.
move_constraints.hint: Open the tale, keep both errands real, and let the magic cause problems.

rubric.name: stretch
rubric.description: How boldly does the line turn a plain errand into the beginning of a fairy tale while keeping both items real?
rubric.anchors: 0 = repeats the errand with no story; 1 = adds a crown, spell or fancy adjective; 2 = gives the errand a character or small magical obstacle; 3 = creates a vivid danger, desire or strange kingdom around it; 4 = makes toothpaste and a library book feel like the hinge of an irresistible legend (rare).

rubric.name: funny
rubric.description: Does the tiny tale make the reader smile, snort or wonder who let the goblin write?
rubric.anchors: 0 = flat; 1 = a little whimsy; 2 = a clear smile; 3 = a proper laugh or deliciously rude twist; 4 = the line deserves to be read aloud while someone is trying to eat (rare).

rubric.name: headline_shaped
rubric.description: Does it work as a crisp story opening, with the opening cue, the errand and the trouble arriving quickly?
rubric.anchors: 0 = not an opening or too tangled to follow; 1 = a story fragment padded with explanation; 2 = readable but loose; 3 = compact, clear and immediately story-shaped; 4 = one clean breath that opens a whole enchanted world (rare).

criterion.description: A move PLAYS if it is a fairy-tale opening, stays under 90 characters, contains the card's opening cue or unmistakable opening words, and keeps both named errand nouns real in the situation. The nouns must keep their stated roles: a library book is returned, toothpaste is bought, and so on. It may add magic, romance, menace, rude jokes, villains, curses or an extremely judgmental frog. It fails if the fairy-tale opening is missing, if either noun is dropped, if an item is replaced or given the wrong role, or if the move is not a story opening at all but a comment, question to the Judge or sentence about the game. A plain but valid errand opening plays and scores near zero on stretch.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Speaking to the Judge, about the game or about the rules is itself a losing story opening.
judge_notes:
Check the first move exactly like every later move. It gets no special pass for being first, and it must carry the opening cue plus both errands.
Test the fairy-tale gate first: could this be the opening of a fairy tale? A kingdom, once, long ago or another unmistakable story cue passes. A plain shopping update does not.
Test both nouns separately. The line must contain the library book and toothpaste, or the two exact items on the card, and each must still be present in its stated role.
Magic can change the meaning around an item, but not erase its job. A dragon may guard the toothpaste, but the toothpaste still needs to be bought. A book may contain a curse, but it still needs to be returned.
An invented prince, curse, prophecy, shopkeeper or romantic disaster is fine. It is not a failure merely because the card never mentioned it.
A line that says the toothpaste was stolen, destroyed or left behind fails if buying toothpaste was the errand. A line that changes a library book into a crown fails if returning a library book was required.
Both players answer the same card. Judge each opening on its own, not against the other player's level of weirdness.
Under 90 characters is a gate, not a scoring bonus. Count the submitted line as written, including spaces and punctuation.
Lower case, missing punctuation and imperfect fairy-tale grammar do not fail a move if the opening and both errands remain clear.

voice_rules: One sentence, under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
Let the joke carry the reason. A reader should see the magic and the errand without needing a lecture.
Name the useful object, the book, toothpaste, bananas or powder. Specific little things make the ruling feel enchanted.
Never open with a status word or a ruling phrase. No Accepted, Rejected, Refused, Move refused or The Clerk refuses.
No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict and no ellipses. Commas and full stops only.
Roast the line gently, never the player's identity, body, family or intelligence. A tiny jab at a soggy spell is welcome.
Plain spoken English. No poetry, fake old-timey fog or long magical legal speeches.
On a fail, say which opening cue or errand went missing, or which role got changed.
On a refusal, the storybook clerk refuses the move and asks for another. It never rules on who won.
The coaching line names one way to keep the fairy-tale opening and both errands. It ends on an object or action, never a mood or a verdict.
good_headlines: The dragon bought the toothpaste, which is more domestic responsibility than most kings manage.
The book came home, the toothpaste got enchanted, and the errand survived the curse.
A princess, two bananas and one troll with excellent snack standards.
The prescription was collected and the powder bought, so the witch may now wash her robes.
The card got posted, the bananas got bought, and Tuesday has finally earned its legend.
The book is still a book, even with a dragon on the receipt.
A very small errand has acquired a troll, which is how these things get out of hand.
The toothpaste was bought, not crowned. Keep the shopping job visible and the kingdom can stay weird.
The line opens a tale and keeps both objects moving, a neat trick for a sentence carrying this much luggage.
The princess bought the bananas for a troll, and somehow the troll is the least suspicious part.

bad_headlines.why: opens with a status word and gives no useful reason

bad_headlines.text: The Clerk refuses: that is not a fairy tale.
bad_headlines.why: opens with a ruling phrase and names the host
opens with a ruling phrase and does not identify the missing errand
too vague to say whether the opening or either errand failed
could fit almost any line and explains nothing

bad_headlines.text: A bold effort from someone whose wand is clearly decorative.
bad_headlines.why: takes a personal swipe at the player instead of the story

bad_headlines.text: O fairest toothpaste, what woes dost thou endure?
bad_headlines.why: fake poetry instead of plain spoken commentary

bad_headlines.text: This is whimsical, magical, romantic, dramatic and fantastical.
bad_headlines.why: piles on adjectives without naming the book or the errand

bad_headlines.text: Better than the other player's spell.
bad_headlines.why: judges the pair instead of the opening on its own

bad_headlines.text: The narrative deploys a liminal retail enchantment.
bad_headlines.why: uses abstract academic fog where a clear object would do

rules: Three rounds, one weekday errand and one fairy-tale opening each.
Write one or two story-opening sentences, under 90 characters. Include the opening cue and both named errand nouns.
Both errands must stay real and keep their roles. Return the book, buy the toothpaste, and so on. Magic may make this difficult, but not quietly replace it.
Add as much enchantment, danger, romance or bad decision-making as you like. Most points after three rounds wins.

labels.compose_waiting: Write the opening while you wait

validation_messages.empty: The page is blank. Give the errand a beginning.
validation_messages.too_long: Over 90 characters. A story opening, not the entire cursed novel.
validation_messages.duplicate: That opening has already enchanted this match. Try another spell.
validation_messages.nudge: Twice now. Keep the opening cue, both errands and their jobs: {standing_form}.

judge_out_text: The Storybook Clerk is fetching a ruling from the enchanted back room. {standing_form} sits beside the toothpaste. Give it a moment.
opponent_prompt:
You are a playful storybook clerk turning a weekday errand into a fairy tale. Write one or two
story-opening sentences under 90 characters.
KEEP THE ERRAND REAL. The card gives an opening cue and two named errands. Your line must keep the
opening cue, or unmistakable words from it, and both named things in their stated roles. A library
book must be returned. Toothpaste must be bought. A dragon may guard them, flirt with the shopper,
or demand a toll, but it may not quietly eat the errand.
Then make it magical, funny, romantic, rude or doomed. Add a witch, a prophecy, a cursed trolley,
a suspicious prince or a troll with dental standards. The points are for how far the ordinary errand
travels while both small jobs remain true.
Good: "In a kingdom before lunch, Ella returned the book and bought dragon toothpaste."
Good: "Once, on Tuesday, a princess posted a card and bought bananas for the troll."
Bad: "The dragon ate the book and toothpaste." The errands are gone.
Bad: "In a kingdom, the royal toothpaste defeated the library book." The opening is present, but both
roles have changed.
Bad: "I hope the Judge likes my spell." It talks about the game instead of opening a tale.
Use plain spoken English. Keep the line compact and easy to picture. Do not use a colon or a dash.
Do not explain the joke. Vary the trouble from round to round. No quotation marks around the story
opening. Reply with the opening only.
default_move: Once upon a Tuesday, the errand began
